slides.title: Chapter 1: Introduction
slides.sub: What Bitcoin is, what it is made of, and why every part of it exists

items.body: Picture: gold coin on circuit traces, from the owner's 2025 Chapter 1 deck. Python 3.14.6; every result on a slide was computed, not typed.

slides.notes: This deck introduces Bitcoin through true stories, the chapter's key concepts with everyday comparisons, and fifteen short programs. Every number on a result picture was computed with the chapter's own Python library.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.sub: Six parts; every number is a slide you can jump to

items.label: code examples with a picture of each result

slides.notes: The route has six parts that follow the order of the chapter. Nine true stories and fifteen code examples are spread across them. The examples are listed in the same order in the chapter code tab of the course page, so every listing here can be run and edited there.
slides.take: Six parts, fifteen examples, nine true stories

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.sub: Each has an answer on a slide; we return to them in the summary

items: Where did Bitcoin come from, and what did it combine?
What is the unit of its money, and who decides how much exists?
Who sets the price, and how does a double-spend get refused?
What do the kinds of wallet differ in, and who controls the keys?
What are an address and an invoice, and how does a wallet send with change?
What can payment channels do that the chain alone cannot?

slides.notes: These six questions are the chapter's own, rewritten so that each has an answer on a slide. We return to them in the summary. A reader who can answer all six has understood the chapter.

slides.title: One chapter, six branches
slides.sub: The concept map the whole deck hangs on
slides.notes: Chapter 1 says that Bitcoin is a collection of concepts and technologies that form the basis of a digital money ecosystem. The six branches are money, network, wallet, usage, foundations and nature. This deck regroups them into six parts.
slides.take: Six branches; every slide today lives on this map

slides.title: Origins
slides.sub: Bitcoin combines old parts, like a recipe of familiar ingredients.

items.meaning: Block 0 carries a newspaper headline dated 3 January 2009.
items.analogy: Think of a time capsule sealed with that day's paper.

items.meaning: Satoshi sent ten bitcoin to Hal Finney nine days later.
items.analogy: Think of the first coin dropped into a new machine.

items.meaning: Chaum, Back, Dai and Szabo each built a part first.
items.analogy: Think of the wheel, chain and frame before the bicycle.

slides.notes: Bitcoin did not appear from nothing. This part reads the first block, follows the first payment and meets the cryptographers whose parts Nakamoto combined.

slides.title: Origins: key concepts
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Introduction
items.meaning: The chapter that says what Bitcoin is and why it matters.
items.analogy: Think of the welcome page of a guidebook, before the maps.

items.label: History of Bitcoin
items.meaning: The path from earlier digital money to the first block in January 2009.
items.analogy: Think of a family tree that shows who the new member descends from.

slides.notes: These cards cover Introduction and History of Bitcoin. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A newspaper headline carved into block zero
slides.sub: Recorded: 3 January 2009

items.cap: Block 0 hex dump - Yusuf Altunel, CC BY 4.0

items: WHAT: The first Bitcoin block carries a newspaper headline: The Times, 3 January 2009, Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks.
WHY: The headline proves the block was not made earlier, and it records the banking crisis that Bitcoin answers.
HOW: Satoshi typed the text into the coinbase script of block 0, the 69 bytes the next code slide reads.

slides.notes: A true story, dated 3 January 2009. Satoshi Nakamoto, the pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin, mined block 0 and wrote the headline of that morning's Times into it. The block is a timestamp and a manifesto.

slides.title: The headline inside block zero
slides.sub: Reading the first block's script as bytes

groups.note: The first block keeps a short script, and the headline sits at its end.
Eight bytes of pushes come first; the rest is the newspaper headline.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - the chapter library of the page supplies the helper functions

items.body: Result: the 77 bytes of block 0's script
It reads: The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks.

slides.notes: The first block keeps a short script. Eight bytes of pushes come first, then 69 bytes of text. Decode them and you read The Times of 3 January 2009 inside the chain itself. It is example 1 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The first block carries its own date: a newspaper headline

slides.title: The first person ever paid in bitcoin
slides.sub: Satoshi Nakamoto, and the cryptographer who ran the code

items.cap: Hal Finney, 1972 - Daily News-Post, public domain

items: WHAT: Nine days after block 0, Satoshi Nakamoto sent 10 bitcoin to Hal Finney in block 170, the first payment between two people.
WHY: Finney had answered the white paper with curiosity and had built the first reusable proof-of-work system years before.
HOW: Finney ran the software and wrote 'Running bitcoin'; the coins reached him directly, with no bank in between.

slides.notes: A true story, dated 12 January 2009. Hal Finney, who had worked on PGP, was the first person besides Satoshi to run Bitcoin and the first to be paid. One peer paid another, directly.

slides.title: Forty years of failed digital money
slides.sub: Every part existed before Bitcoin combined them

items.cap: David Chaum, 2018 - Harry Murphy, CC BY 2.0

items: WHAT: David Chaum, Adam Back, Wei Dai and Nick Szabo each built a part of digital money between 1982 and 1998.
WHY: Their systems failed or stayed unbuilt, because none could agree on one history without a trusted leader.
HOW: Nakamoto's white paper of 31 October 2008 cites them and adds proof of work as the voting weight of an open network.

slides.notes: A true story, dated 31 October 2008. Chaum's company DigiCash went bankrupt; Back's Hashcash priced email with work; b-money and bit gold were never built. Nakamoto added the missing piece and combined them.

slides.title: Four near misses, one combination
slides.sub: Each part existed before Bitcoin joined them

items: DigiCash went bankrupt; b-money and bit gold were never built.
Agreement without a leader was the missing piece.

slides.notes: Chaum's ecash of 1982, Back's Hashcash of 1997, and the b-money and bit gold of 1998 each solved a piece. Nakamoto's paper of 2008 combined them with proof of work as the vote. The genesis block ran in 2009.
slides.take: The pieces were old; the combination was new

slides.title: Money and price
slides.sub: Money is a ledger of who owns what; Bitcoin keeps that ledger in public.

items.meaning: Stones, coins, notes and bank balances are all ledgers.
items.analogy: Think of a scoreboard that everyone agrees to trust.

items.meaning: One coin divides into 100 million satoshis; the cap is 21 million.
items.analogy: Think of a cake cut into a hundred million crumbs.

items.meaning: Markets set the price; exchanges and ATMs convert it.
items.analogy: Think of a market stall whose prices change by the hour.

slides.notes: Money is a ledger. We see old forms of money, count in satoshis, run the supply schedule and watch a price being discovered by trades, never declared.

slides.title: Money and price: key concepts
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: floating exchange rate
items.meaning: The price of bitcoin is set by markets and moves with supply and demand.
items.analogy: Think of the price of tomatoes at a stall, which moves with the harvest and the crowd.

items.label: Finding the Current Price of Bitcoin
items.meaning: Exchanges quote prices; a volume-weighted average gives one fair daily figure.
items.analogy: Think of reading the board of a stock exchange instead of asking one trader.

items.label: currency exchange
items.meaning: A market where buyers and sellers swap bitcoin and local money, with identity checks.
items.analogy: Think of the money-changer's booth at an airport.

items.label: Bitcoin ATM
items.meaning: A machine that takes cash and sends bitcoin to your phone wallet.
items.analogy: Think of a vending machine that sells coins instead of snacks.

slides.notes: These cards cover floating exchange rate, Finding the Current Price of Bitcoin, currency exchange and Bitcoin ATM. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: The island where money never moved
slides.sub: Documented in 1903; the free ebook edition came in 2024

items.cap: Yap stone money - Eric Guinther, CC BY-SA 3.0

items: WHAT: On Yap, wealth was held in limestone discs called rai, up to four metres wide, that never moved when they changed owner.
WHY: What changed was the shared memory of who owned each stone, so the stone worked as a public ledger.
HOW: Anthropologist William Henry Furness III described it after visiting in 1903; a stone that sank at sea was still traded.

items.linkText: Furness: The Island of Stone Money (book)

slides.notes: A true story, documented in 1903. On the island of Yap the stones stayed where they lay and the community remembered who owned them. Money is a ledger, and Bitcoin makes the shared memory digital.

slides.title: Five thousand years to digital cash
slides.sub: From grain ledgers to pure fiat money, 3000 BCE to 1971

items.cap: Electrum stater, 600-550 BCE - Cleveland Museum of Art, CC0

items: WHAT: On 15 August 1971 President Richard Nixon cut the dollar's last tie to gold, leaving pure fiat money.
WHY: Grain ledgers, Lydian coins, paper notes and bank balances are all ledgers; they differ in who keeps them.
HOW: Cards and online banking made money digital as entries in private ledgers; Bitcoin makes the ledger public.

slides.notes: A true story, dated 15 August 1971. Money kept changing form, from Mesopotamian grain entries to Lydian coins to bank balances. Cryptocurrency is the next step: a ledger that no single institution keeps.

slides.title: Traditional, digital, crypto: side by side
slides.sub: The chapter's one table: same uses, different ledgers

rows: Commercial banks on a central bank base
No one - issuance is in the protocol
No ledger - possession is the record
Peer to peer, in about an hour

slides.notes: Read down a column to see one kind of money, and across a row to see which property changes. Who keeps the ledger is the row that matters most in this course.
slides.take: Same uses, different ledgers: that difference is this course

slides.title: The internet got payments - and new gatekeepers
slides.sub: The dot-com boom digitised paying, not cash

items.cap: PayPal logo - PayPal, public domain

items: WHAT: On 8 July 2002 eBay agreed to buy PayPal for 1.5 billion dollars, ending the dot-com race to pay online.
WHY: Online payment was solved only as accounts on one company's private ledger; the internet still had no cash.
HOW: Confinity (Levchin, Thiel, 1998) and X.com (Musk, 1999) merged in 2000; Beenz and Flooz died in the 2001 crash.

slides.notes: A true story, dated 8 July 2002. The web could sell before it could pay. PayPal solved it by adding a middleman, and the pure digital currencies of the boom failed.

slides.title: When the money in your hand stops working
slides.sub: Ukraine, February 2022: a state turns to an open payment network

items.cap: Fedorov - U.S. Embassy Kyiv, PD

items: WHAT: On 26 February 2022 Ukraine's government posted crypto donation addresses and, with an aid group, raised 54.7 million dollars in about a week.
WHY: With war at the capital, ordinary rails were too slow; open digital money kept working where banks, cards or cash stopped.
HOW: Fedorov's ministry of digital transformation published the addresses, and CNBC reported the total on 3 March 2022.

slides.notes: A true story, dated 26 February 2022. Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine's minister of digital transformation, published donation addresses. The next slide lists four more documented cases from 2007 to 2018.

slides.title: When the money in your hand stops working
slides.sub: Five documented cases, five links; no hypotheticals

items.cap: Kenya: Fiona Graham / WorldRemit, CC BY-SA 2.0
Cyprus: Martin Addison, CC BY-SA 2.0
Greece: Norbert Nagel, CC BY-SA 3.0
Venezuela: Rjcastillo, CC BY-SA 4.0
Ukraine: U.S. Embassy Kyiv, public domain

groups.head: Banks, cards or cash stopped serving people
rows: No banks for most adults - M-Pesa made phones the payment rail
Banks shut for days; a levy took part of deposits overnight
Capital controls: ATM withdrawals capped at 60 euros a day

groups.head: A currency or a state failed
rows: Hyperinflation beyond 1,000,000% - wages melted in hours
State and NGO raised $54.7M in crypto in a week

slides.notes: Kenya 2007, Cyprus 2013, Greece 2015, Venezuela 2018 and Ukraine 2022. In each case banks, cards or cash stopped serving people. Each line links to its source.
slides.take: Crisis or war, banked or not: the need is documented

slides.title: A bitcoin counted in satoshis
slides.sub: The unit and its smallest piece

groups.note: A bitcoin is counted in whole satoshis, one hundred million to the coin.
Three common amounts, each written as a count of satoshis.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - the chapter library of the page supplies the helper functions

items.body: Result: the same value in three units
0.001 bitcoin is exactly 100,000 satoshis, so every amount is a whole number.

slides.notes: A bitcoin divides into 100 million satoshis. We multiply 0.001 by that number and get exactly 100,000. Amounts in the protocol are whole satoshis, never fractions. It is example 2 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Money here is counting, and the units are exact

slides.title: The subsidy at five block heights
slides.sub: New bitcoin per block, halved every 210,000 blocks

groups.note: The subsidy starts at fifty bitcoin and halves every 210,000 blocks.

rows: ratios = [a / b for a, b in zip(subs, subs[1:])]
groups.note: Each era pays exactly half of the era before it.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - the chapter library of the page supplies the helper functions

items.body: Result: subsidy in bitcoin, by halving year
Each era pays half of the one before: 50, 25, 12.5, 6.25, and since April 2024 3.125.

slides.notes: The block subsidy starts at fifty bitcoin. The code shifts it right once per era. Five heights give the staircase from 2009 to 2024, each step exactly half of the one before. It is example 3 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Every halving cuts new issuance in half

slides.title: The 21 million cap is a sum
slides.sub: Issuance by era, added up by the code

rows: eras = [(50 * COIN >> k) * HALVING for k in range(33)]
groups.note: Each era issues its subsidy for 210,000 blocks, then the subsidy halves.
Adding every era gives the cap, just under 21 million bitcoin.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - the chapter library of the page supplies the helper functions

items.body: Result: bitcoin issued after each era, in millions
The total creeps toward 21 million; the cap is 20999999.9769 bitcoin.

slides.notes: Each era issues its subsidy over 210,000 blocks. Adding 33 eras gives 20,999,999.9769 bitcoin. The chart shows the running total approaching 21 million without reaching it. It is example 4 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Scarcity is arithmetic that every node can re-run

slides.title: No one sets the price: trades do
slides.sub: A price is a ratio; a day's figure is a weighted average

rows: prices = [round(u / b, 2) for b, u in trades]
groups.note: Three illustrative trades: bitcoin bought, and the dollars paid for it.

rows: avg = round(vwap([(b, u / b) for b, u in trades]), 2)
groups.note: The day's single figure weights each price by its volume.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - the chapter library of the page supplies the helper functions

items.body: Result: dollars paid per bitcoin
Each trade sets its own price; the volume-weighted day average is 62,764.71 dollars.

slides.notes: Each trade has its own price, found by dividing dollars by bitcoin. A volume-weighted average gives one fair figure for the day. The three trades are illustrative, not market data. It is example 5 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Everyone who trades sets the price a little

slides.title: Two pizzas for ten thousand bitcoin
slides.sub: 22 May 2010: the day a price began to exist

items.cap: Papa John's plaque - Sanjev Rajaram, CC0

items: WHAT: On 22 May 2010 Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoin for two Papa John's pizzas, the first known commercial purchase in bitcoin.
WHY: Until then nobody knew what a bitcoin was worth; this purchase is the day a floating price began to exist.
HOW: He offered the coins on the bitcointalk forum, and student Jeremy Sturdivant ordered the pizzas for delivery to Jacksonville.

slides.notes: A true story, dated 22 May 2010. Laszlo Hanyecz offered 10,000 bitcoin for two pizzas on a forum and Jeremy Sturdivant ordered them. Price is discovered the first time someone actually pays.

slides.title: The Pizza Day coins, repriced
slides.sub: 10,000 bitcoin at six documented moments

rows: val = {d: int(coins * p) for d, p in PIZZA.items()}
groups.note: Ten thousand bitcoin, priced at six documented moments.
The dollar value of the same coins at each moment, from 2010 to 2026.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - the chapter library of the page supplies the helper functions

items.body: Result: value of the 10,000 BTC, in dollars (log axis)

items.title: Value of 10,000 BTC in dollars (log axis)

items.body: The same coins grew by a factor of 20,831,463, from $41 to $854M.

slides.notes: The pizzas cost 41 dollars of bitcoin in May 2010. The same coins at five later milestones draw the chart; the last point is the price fetched on 6 October 2026. Each gridline is ten times more. It is example 6 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: From 41 dollars to 854 million: price discovery never stopped

slides.title: The network
slides.sub: No bank sits in the middle: shared rules and shared work do its job.

items.meaning: Every node checks the same rules, so none is in charge.
items.analogy: Think of neighbours who all keep a copy of the land register.

items.meaning: Proof of work makes honest history cheap to check.
items.analogy: Think of a lock that took a day to make and a second to inspect.

items.meaning: Fees pay miners; each new block makes a payment safer.
items.analogy: Think of a courier's tip and cement poured over a footprint.

slides.notes: No bank stands in the middle. Every node checks the same rules, proof of work makes history costly to forge, and fees and confirmations settle payments.

slides.title: A bank in the middle against peers
slides.sub: Decentralisation is an architecture, not a slogan

right.title: Bitcoin: every node checks every rule

slides.notes: On the left one ledger-keeper sees everything and everyone depends on it. On the right every node checks every rule. Remove one node and the network goes on.
slides.take: Remove any one node and the network still agrees

slides.title: The network: key concepts (1 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: proof of work
items.meaning: Adding a block costs real computation, and anyone can check it cheaply.
items.analogy: Think of a jigsaw puzzle: hard to solve, a glance to see it is done.

items.label: consensus
items.meaning: Every node applies the same rules, so all agree on one history without a leader.
items.analogy: Think of neighbours who all keep the same record of who owns which field.

items.label: double-spend
items.meaning: Spending one unit of digital money twice; the network refuses the second try.
items.analogy: Think of photocopying a banknote and paying with both.

slides.notes: These cards cover proof of work, consensus and double-spend. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Hard to find, easy to check
slides.sub: A toy proof of work with hexadecimal zeros

groups.note: Search for a number that gives a hash starting with zeros.
Anyone checks the winner with one hash instead of a long search.
The last line shows how many guesses each difficulty took.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - the chapter library of the page supplies the helper functions

items.body: Result: guesses needed (log axis)
Each extra zero makes the search about sixteen times longer on average; checking stays one hash.

slides.notes: The search tries numbers until the hash starts with zeros. Each extra zero makes it about sixteen times longer on average. Anyone checks the winner with a single hash. It is example 7 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Finding takes thousands of guesses; checking takes one hash

slides.title: Mining pays for honesty
slides.sub: New coin and fees reward the work that secures the chain

items: The subsidy follows the halving chart
Cheating costs more than it could win
Chapter 12 opens the mechanism

items.cap: from the owner's 2025 deck

slides.notes: Transactions wait, miners spend energy on proof of work, a block is found about every ten minutes, and the finder earns subsidy plus fees. Cheating costs more than it could win.
slides.take: Security is bought with energy and paid in bitcoin

slides.title: Why digital money had to wait
slides.sub: The copy problem: a digital coin is a file

items: Make money digital and it becomes a file
Files copy perfectly, so coins would too
Both copies get spent: the double-spend
Only a trusted central ledger could stop it

slides.notes: A digital coin is only a file, and files copy perfectly. Both copies could be spent. For decades only a trusted central ledger could stop that, so digital money meant bank money.
slides.take: A file can be copied; a coin must not be

slides.title: The double-spend, solved in public
slides.sub: One shared ledger, one agreed order, no referee

items: Every payment is broadcast to every node
Nodes agree on one order for all payments
The first spend of a coin enters the block
The second is refused by every node

slides.notes: Every payment is broadcast and the nodes agree on one order. The first spend of a coin enters the block, and every node refuses the second. The next code slide runs that rule.
slides.take: Agreement on order is what removes the referee

slides.title: A double spend is refused
slides.sub: One shared ledger, one rule, no referee

groups.note: A shared ledger remembers which coins are spent.
Alice offers the same coin again; the rule says no, with no referee.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - the chapter library of the page supplies the helper functions

items.body: Result: two payments of the same coin
The first spend is recorded; the same coin offered again is refused by the rule alone.

slides.notes: A ledger remembers which coins are spent. Alice pays Bob with coin c1 and it is accepted. When she offers the same coin to Carol, the rule refuses it. No bank decides. It is example 8 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The second spend of a coin is refused everywhere

slides.title: A chain that notices tampering
slides.sub: Each block hashes its text with the block before

groups.note: Three blocks, each hashing its own text together with the block before.
Change one word in block two; the check stops there.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - the chapter library of the page supplies the helper functions

items.body: Result: does each block's link still hold?
Changing block two breaks its link, so block two and everything after it are no longer trusted.

slides.notes: Each block's hash covers its own text and the hash of the block before. Changing one word in block two makes the check stop there, so nothing after it can be trusted. It is example 9 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Change one old block and every later link fails

slides.title: The network: key concepts (2 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: confirmation
items.meaning: Each block added after a payment makes the payment harder to reverse.
items.analogy: Think of another layer of cement poured over a footprint.

items.label: transaction fee
items.meaning: The amount a sender adds for the miner who puts the payment in a block.
items.analogy: Think of a tip for the courier who picks your parcel for the next van.

slides.notes: These cards cover confirmation and transaction fee. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 1.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: What the outputs leave over is the fee
slides.sub: A transaction has no fee field; the difference is the fee

groups.note: One coin of 100,000 satoshis pays Bob and sends the change back.
Whatever the outputs do not take goes to the miner as the fee.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - the chapter library of the page supplies the helper functions

items.body: Result: where the 100,000 satoshis go
The fee is 5,000 satoshis, 5.0 percent of the coin; no output carries it.

slides.notes: A coin of 100,000 satoshis pays 20,000 to Bob and returns 75,000 as change. The 5,000 left over goes to the miner who includes the payment. Fees are implied, never written. It is example 10 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The fee is the part of the coin nobody was given

slides.title: Wallets and keys
slides.sub: A wallet holds keys, not coins, like a ring of keys to many safes.

items.meaning: Desktop, mobile, web and hardware wallets differ in risk.
items.analogy: Think of a pocket, a safe and a cloakroom ticket.

items.meaning: A full node checks everything; a light client trusts others.
items.analogy: Think of an auditor beside a tourist with a map.

items.meaning: Whoever holds the keys controls the coins; a recovery code restores them.
items.analogy: Think of a spare key kept in a bank locker.

slides.notes: A wallet holds keys, not coins. This part sorts wallets by platform, by how much of the network they check, and by who holds the keys and the backup.

slides.title: The wallet branch, mapped
slides.sub: Four questions about any wallet: platform, node, keys, backup
slides.notes: A wallet is classified by its platform, by how much of the network it checks, by who holds the keys, and by how it is backed up. Every leaf has a card in this part.
slides.take: Four questions place any wallet on this map

slides.title: Wallets and keys: key concepts (1 of 4)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Getting Started
items.meaning: The first decisions: what a wallet is and which one to choose.
items.analogy: Think of choosing a bag before you go shopping.

items.label: Choosing a Bitcoin Wallet
items.meaning: Pick a wallet by who holds the keys, which device it runs on, and how far you trust it.
items.analogy: Think of choosing between a pocket, a home safe and a bank locker.

items.label: Types of Bitcoin wallets
items.meaning: Desktop, mobile, web and hardware signing devices, each with its own trade-offs.
items.analogy: Think of a bicycle, a car and a bus: all travel, with different limits.

items.label: desktop wallet
items.meaning: The first kind of wallet, run on Windows, macOS or Linux.

slides.title: Your key is your deed
slides.sub: With a house the key opens and the registry proves; in Bitcoin the key does both

items: Bitcoin's trick: a signature proves you hold the key while the key stays secret

slides.notes: Access to bitcoin is controlled by private keys, like very long PINs. With a house, the key opens the door and a registry proves the owner. In Bitcoin the key is both, so it must prove without being shown.
slides.take: Prove you hold the key; never reveal it

slides.title: Whoever holds the keys holds the coins

rows: You trust their honesty and uptime

slides.notes: With full control you keep the keys, sign yourself and carry the backup. With third-party control a service keeps the keys, which is convenient, and you trust its honesty and uptime. Every wallet type can be either.
slides.take: Custody is the first security decision you make

slides.title: The exchange that lost everyone's coins
slides.sub: Tokyo, February 2014: balances on a website, keys elsewhere

items.cap: Mt. Gox logo - author unknown, public domain

items: WHAT: On 28 February 2014 Mt. Gox of Tokyo filed for bankruptcy and admitted that about 850,000 bitcoin were gone.
WHY: Customers had balances on a website, but the keys, and so the coins, were in someone else's hands all along.
HOW: The exchange of chief executive Mark Karpeles filed at the Tokyo District Court; creditors were still being repaid a decade later.

slides.notes: A true story, dated 28 February 2014. Mt. Gox was once the largest bitcoin exchange. Whoever holds the keys holds the coins, exchanges included. This is the cost of a custodial wallet.

slides.title: A recovery phrase becomes a seed
slides.sub: Key stretching repeats a hash, 2048 times in BIP 39

groups.note: The test phrase of BIP 39: eleven times abandon, then about.

rows: seeds = [stretch(TEST_PHRASE, n)[:8] for n in rounds]
groups.note: Stretching repeats the hash; the wallet uses 2048 rounds.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - the chapter library of the page supplies the helper functions

items.body: Result: the same twelve words, three round counts
More rounds give an unrelated seed; wallets use 2048, so every guess costs 2048 rounds.

slides.notes: A recovery phrase of twelve words is stretched by repeating a keyed hash. With 1, 10 or 2048 rounds the seeds look unrelated. A thief guessing phrases pays all 2048 rounds per guess. It is example 11 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Slow on purpose: every guess costs the full 2048 rounds

slides.sub: How the address of the first block is built

items.body: Result: the address of block 0, in parts
The 25 bytes are written in Base58 as the 34-character address 1A1zP1eP5QGefi2DMPTfTL5SLmv7DivfNa.

slides.notes: Block 0 pays to a 20-byte key hash behind a version byte. The checksum is the first four bytes of a double hash. Together they make 25 bytes, written in Base58 as a 34-character address. It is example 12 in the chapter code tab of the course page.

slides.title: Sending: coins in, payment and change out

slides.title: Foundations
slides.sub: Two old solved problems, joined into one system, like two rivers.

items.meaning: Hashcash made messages cost work; the generals agreed without trust.
items.analogy: Think of two rivers that meet in one channel.

items.meaning: Payment channels keep most payments off the public ledger.
items.analogy: Think of a bar tab settled once at closing time.

items.meaning: Virtual, borderless, decentralized and robust, by design.
items.analogy: Think of a public library no single person owns.

slides.notes: Two old ideas, proof of work and agreement without trust, meet in Bitcoin. Payment channels keep many payments off the chain, and four adjectives name its nature.

slides.title: Two solved problems, one new system
slides.sub: 1997 and 1982 meet in 2008

items.head: Hashcash (1997)
items.body: Proof-of-work: make sending cost a computation, so flooding costs real resources. Bitcoin turns the same cost into the price of writing history.

items.head: Byzantine Generals (1982)
items.body: How do parties that cannot trust each other agree on one message? Proof-of-work plus the longest valid chain is Bitcoin's practical answer.

slides.notes: Hashcash of 1997 makes sending cost computation. The Byzantine Generals' problem of 1982 asks how parties that cannot trust each other agree. Proof of work with the longest valid chain is Bitcoin's practical answer.
slides.take: Neither idea was new; their combination was

slides.notes: The chapter gives two answers. Bitcoin is virtual, borderless, decentralized and robust, and it is built from a peer-to-peer protocol, a public journal and a consensus rule set. Each adjective is engineered.

slides.title: The chapter in six lines
slides.sub: One line per part, each provable from its slides

items: Origins: a dated headline sits in block 0, and the first payment went from person to person.
Money is a ledger; the cap of 21 million is arithmetic, and the price is discovered by trades.
The network has no bank: every node checks every rule, and proof of work makes history costly.
A wallet holds keys, not coins; whoever holds the keys holds the coins, and the code restores them.
A first payment needs an address or invoice, whole coins, change, and a fee for the miner.
Foundations: two old ideas joined, and payment channels that keep many payments off the chain.
